payload.rationale: Observed facts: BLS reported August payroll growth of 162,000 with unemployment at 4.1%, while June and July were revised down to 31,000 and 21,000 respectively (three-month average ~71,000). September FOMC projections imply a broadly stable labor market (Q4 unemployment median 4.1%, GDP growth 2.3%), which is consistent with modest positive payroll gains rather than contraction. Transfer assumptions: I treat the underlying trend for October's first print as roughly 50,000–80,000 with a monthly standard deviation around 70,000–80,000 (recent volatility plus first-print noise). Under that distribution, the chance the first print exceeds 30,000 is roughly 60–75%. I shade toward the middle because two of the last three months landed below the threshold after revision and downward revisions suggest initial prints have been running hot relative to truth, while the contract resolves on the initial October print (which historically has a mild upward bias versus revised figures, helping YES). Why too high: the trend could be closer to the June–July pace (~25,000), in which case the outcome is near a coin flip; October-specific shocks (strikes, hurricanes, a federal shutdown affecting payroll counts) could depress the print; the 162k August figure may itself be revised or be an outlier. Why too low: 162k may signal reacceleration, unemployment is stable, first prints tend to skew higher than later revisions, and a 30,000 bar is low relative to any plausible positive trend. Net estimate ~0.67.
limitations: September and October data are unknown; only three payroll readings supplied.
No information on strikes, weather, government shutdown risk, or birth-death model changes that could distort October's print.
Assumed trend and volatility parameters are judgmental, not from a fitted model.
Q4 unemployment projection is a quarterly average from a different survey and is only weakly informative about October payrolls.
